sources.text: Swimming. Club squad, mainly 100 metre freestyle. We have a local meet on November 2. I swim other events too, but this is my focus.
sources.question: What sport are we focusing on right now?

sources.text: I want a personal best in the 100 freestyle. I care about competing, even if I am quiet. I also want time for family, cooking and friends.
sources.question: What would you love to achieve in your sport, and why does it matter to you?

sources.text: I keep my pace through the middle better now. My last two coached race-pace sets were more even than the earlier ones. I do not have the split sheet with me, so please do not put exact numbers on it.
sources.question: What feels strongest about the way you are performing right now?

sources.text: The turn unsettles me. If it feels wrong I keep thinking about it during the next length. I want to understand what to change rather than check everything.
sources.question: What part of your performance would you most like to improve?

sources.text: At the November meet I want to stay with my race after a turn I do not like. A personal best would be great, but handling that moment is something I can work on first.
sources.question: What would make the next six to eight weeks feel successful in your sport?

sources.text: Four pool sessions: Monday, Tuesday, Thursday and Saturday, 75 minutes each. Coach plans them. I have a short Saturday cafe shift later. Wednesday and Sunday have no scheduled training.
sources.question: What does a normal training week look like for you?

sources.text: I want to know what a useful turn feels like, and carry it into the next length. I do not want to add pool hours during exams.
sources.question: What do you most want your training to help you do better?

sources.text: Watching one clip with my coach the following day helped me see one part of a turn. I used the example in the next session. I still need my coach to tell me what to look for technically.
sources.question: Which part of your training seems to be helping most?

sources.text: At the end of practice I can ask about three different things and come away checking all of them. I wrote a long list once and kept rereading it before a set. That made it harder to settle.
sources.question: Which part feels confusing, hard to keep up with, or not useful?

sources.text: A brief one-to-one explanation and one written thing to try in the existing set. I want the plan decided before the week gets busy. Exams start October 5.
sources.question: What would make your training week work better for you?

sources.text: I am clear about the first thing to do and then I swim. I do not need to talk a lot to feel competitive.
sources.question: When you are playing with confidence, what is different about you?

sources.text: I narrow in on the turn. At the last meet I replayed one missed turn while I still had a length to swim. When someone asked instantly what happened I said fine because I did not have the words yet.
sources.question: When the pressure goes up, what usually happens for you?

sources.text: On the night I need dinner and a break. The next day I can use one clip with my coach. During a race I do not yet have a reset that I trust.
sources.question: After a mistake or a bad performance, what helps you get back into it?

sources.text: Leave one imperfect turn behind and race the length I am in. I would like to test a simple reset, but I do not want someone promising it will fix my time.
sources.question: What would you most like to handle better mentally in your sport?

sources.text: A specific example, preferably privately, and a little time to think. Please do not take silence as agreement. My parents are happy to leave the coaching to the coach.
sources.question: What do you need from the people around you to compete at your best?

sources.text: Grade 11. I am preparing for exams in early October. I am keeping up, but want more quiet revision time for the next few weeks.
sources.question: How is school going for you right now?

sources.text: Biology is going well. In maths I follow a worked example but hesitate on my own. I completed four of six questions independently on the last practice sheet. That is one sheet, not a grade.
sources.question: Which parts of school feel strongest, and which need help?

sources.text: Be able to solve the next set of mixed maths revision questions without needing the first step shown each time.
sources.question: What would you like to achieve in school this term?

sources.text: I might study food or hospitality after school. I have only helped at the cafe twice before this new short shift, so I want to explore before deciding.
sources.question: Where would you like school to lead for you?

sources.text: The four pool sessions fit if no extra hours are added. I have two 40-minute maths revision slots on Wednesday and Sunday. I want to keep those and a quiet evening with family.
sources.question: How are school and sport fitting together in your week?

sources.text: Eli has held a more even pace in the last two race-pace sets. I have seen him continue looking for explanations after a turn. I cannot tell exactly what he thinks during a race.
I would start with one turn focus that I can show him, then observe whether he carries on with the next length. I will choose the technical cue after we look at the example together.
A five-minute discussion can replace the first five minutes of our existing Monday review. It does not add pool time. I can give him one written cue. He has not yet chosen or agreed a reset with me.

bos_sources.headline: Quiet first, firm when it matters
bos_sources.text:
Your quiet side can make your determination less visible than it really is. You often listen, sort out your wording, and only then step in. But once something matters and you have thought it through, you can be competitive, direct, and even stubborn about the choice. With your closest friends, the same person who can miss an opening in class may be the one talking most. Your pace changes with trust, timing, and pressure; it is not the same everywhere.

You are serious about improvement without needing to be the center of attention. You want faster swim times, and getting something a little better can be satisfying even when nobody is watching. At the same time, sport is not meant to swallow your whole life. Family, a couple of close friends, and cooking matter, and you want time left for people even if sport becomes more serious. Choosing fewer weekend shifts protected swimming and friendships, though you still noticed the money you were giving up. You do not make tradeoffs carelessly.

Much of your organization seems connected to care. A phone list, early notice, and a remembered agreement help you be someone other people can plan around. You can rearrange a week when practice changes; what bothers you more is a sudden change that collides with a promise. That makes your structure less about controlling every moment and more about keeping different parts of life from letting each other down. The harder side is that you may say yes to avoid trouble, then end up carrying too much sorting and checking yourself.

Your mind often looks for a solid first foothold. For a difficult choice, you may write down the options, talk to one trusted person, and let the decision sit for a few days. When learning, one worked example or a clear first step gives you something real to test against your own attempt. This does not mean you need full certainty before acting. Trusted company, low stakes, or familiarity can bring out a much more experimental side.

Socially, you seem to want closeness more than constant contact. Small groups suit you, while a large team day can be genuinely fun and still leave you wanting an evening without plans. New people are easier when everyone is doing something together, because the activity gives the meeting a natural shape. Your need for space can grow after a packed schedule, but that does not erase the talkative side that close friends get to see.

You usually make room for people, but you are not only a follower. If a group has no plan, you can suggest one and ask whether it works for everyone. You notice who has not spoken, remember what was agreed, and bring in another person for a useful check. In disagreement, you may wait while an issue seems small. Once you name it, though, you can explain the practical effect and help create a workable agreement. To you, respect seems closely tied to following through and giving honest notice.

Under pressure, your usual broad view can shrink around one mistake. You may still do the other parts, but that one detail keeps pulling your attention back, and being asked to explain immediately can leave your words behind. When upset, you can become even quieter and say you are fine before you are ready. Your way back seems to have stages: ordinary comfort and less analysis first, then one understandable piece to review later. Quiet time, cooking with music, or a walk with one friend can help you feel more like yourself.

Cooking brings many sides of you into the same room. It gives you detail and repetition when you want to master something, freedom when a recipe is familiar, calm when life is crowded, and a possible future worth exploring. You are interested in cooking for a living, but you also know that helping at a café twice is not enough to settle that question. That combination says something important about you: you can care deeply without pretending to be certain. You build clarity so you can commit, then quietly try to make both the work and the people around it more reliable.

bos_sources.headline: More than one finish line
bos_sources.text:
Your life does not seem organized around one role. Swimming matters, but so do family, a couple of close friends, and cooking. You want room for those people even if sport becomes more serious. That is not a lack of ambition; it is a wish for ambition to live inside a fuller life instead of taking every available space.

You have been clear that you like competing and want to improve your times. What matters less is being the person everyone watches. Your drive seems to come more from making progress and meeting your own commitment than from becoming the center of the room. This is why a quiet presentation can give an incomplete picture of how much you care.

Cooking holds an unusual amount of meaning for you. It can be careful craft, a place to experiment, a way to settle after a packed week, and a possible kind of work. You have not turned that interest into a fixed career story: after helping at a café only twice, you know you have more to learn about the work. Your interest is real, and your uncertainty is honest.

Your choice to reduce weekend shifts shows how you are balancing things now: money mattered, but so did swimming and friendship. You still wondered about the money afterward, which suggests that choosing one value does not make the others disappear. Future tradeoffs may look different, but the direction is already clear: success would not feel complete if it left no time for the people and interests that make life yours.
bos_sources.takeaway: You want to improve seriously without shrinking your whole identity to one result.

bos_sources.headline: You make choices visible
bos_sources.text:
When a decision matters, you tend to put it somewhere you can see it. Writing the options down, talking with one person, and taking a few days helped you choose fewer work shifts. This gives several concerns a fair chance to count instead of letting the loudest or nearest one decide everything.

You can keep friendship, sport, money, promises, and future time in mind together. That gives your judgment range, but it can also keep the cost of the unchosen path alive after you have acted. Wondering whether you should have saved more did not undo your choice; it showed that no option protected everything. Sometimes careful thinking may slide into second-guessing.

Learning often becomes easier when you have one concrete starting point. A worked maths example let you try the next problem yourself and compare the result. A complete recipe gives you the shape before you begin. You seem to use a model as a launch point, not as a substitute for your own effort. This may fit step-by-step tasks especially well; other subjects may bring out a different approach.

Preparation is not an absolute rule for you. With a friend and low stakes, you tried kayaking without knowing much. In familiar cooking, you change recipes just to see what happens. Once you know enough to stand on, curiosity can take over from caution. The opposite tradeoff is that a decision you have fully considered may become hard to reopen, even when rearranging ordinary plans is easy.
bos_sources.takeaway: A clear foothold helps you think independently, while settled choices may take more effort to reopen.

bos_sources.headline: Your thoughts need a fair opening
bos_sources.text:
There is often a gap between having a view and getting it into the conversation. You usually have an opinion, but you may still be arranging the words. In a fast class discussion, the opening can close before you are ready. With your two best friends, you can be the person who talks most, so the important difference is not whether you have things to say; it is the setting and the time available.

Feedback works best for you when it contains something usable. Specific, explained, one-to-one comments tell you what worked or what needs changing. “Good job” is pleasant but too vague to guide the next attempt. You can take a direct correction, especially when you are allowed a moment to think instead of having to react on the spot.

When you are upset or under pressure, less of your inner experience may reach other people. You can get quieter, say you are fine too soon, and keep replaying the issue. An instant request for an explanation can make words harder to find. That means someone may hear a shorter answer than the thought behind it, without either side realizing how much is missing.

In disagreement, you may leave a small problem alone at first. When a friend’s changing meeting times kept affecting your plans, you eventually described the effect, heard that he had not realized, and helped agree on a clearer arrangement. In that conversation, waiting did not mean you had no boundary. Still, bringing up a concern earlier may sometimes save you from carrying it privately until it grows.
bos_sources.takeaway: Your view becomes clearer to others when there is enough time, detail, and room to answer honestly.

bos_sources.headline: Closeness grows through doing
bos_sources.text:
You seem to build closeness through a small circle rather than through being socially available all the time. A couple of close friends matter a lot, small groups feel good, and big team days can still be fun. Needing an evening without plans afterward does not cancel the enjoyment; both can be true.

Shared activity makes unfamiliar people easier for you to meet. Working or moving alongside someone gives the interaction a purpose, so connection does not have to begin with instant personal conversation. Trusted company and low stakes may also free your more spontaneous side, although that may not work the same way in every unfamiliar setting.

You also make belonging practical. You notice when someone has not had a turn, invite them in, remember what the group promised, and care about early notice when plans change. Fairness, for you, seems less about everyone always agreeing and more about treating one another’s time and responsibilities as real. You try to offer the same follow-through you want from others.

The tension is that your wish not to cause trouble can make your own limits arrive late. You sometimes say yes and then have too much to sort out, or postpone a small disagreement while it keeps taking up space. A pause can be useful if it helps you choose your words; it is less useful when it only leaves you carrying the inconvenience. With close friends, enough trust may make that boundary easier to show.
bos_sources.takeaway: You build trust through shared time, practical care, and promises people can rely on.

bos_sources.headline: A promise gives work weight
bos_sources.text:
Two things seem to give effort weight for you: improvement and ownership. You like getting something a little better, and you want people to be able to rely on you. Either one can keep you moving. Together, they create a steady kind of persistence that does not need a crowd watching it.

Making the same bread across four weekends was not just repetition; each attempt had a result you cared about refining. A boring part of a class project worked differently. The task itself did not interest you, but it was yours, so finishing still mattered. One effort came from craft, the other from commitment.

Those strengths can compete with your other responsibilities. You can spend too long perfecting one small part, check an email twice and still delay sending it, or say yes before making room for the new promise. The problem is not that detail or reliability is bad. It is that one promise can receive so much protection that the next promise gets less time.

You are not driven only by duty. In familiar cooking, you alter recipes for the fun of finding out what happens. In sport, you genuinely like competition and want better times, even though attention is not the reward you care about most. Your effort is strongest when there is something real to improve, explore, or stand behind—not merely a request to look busy.
bos_sources.takeaway: Improvement and ownership keep you going; the challenge is giving each commitment the right amount of care.

bos_sources.headline: First space, then sense-making
bos_sources.text:
On an ordinary day, you can notice a mistake and move on. Under pressure, that same mistake can keep pulling your attention back. You may still complete the other parts, so this is not a total stop. It is more like the view becomes narrower, with less room left for the whole performance or problem.

Your outside signal may also get smaller while the inside stays busy. You have described becoming quieter, saying you are fine before you are ready, and replaying what happened. If someone asks for words immediately, you may struggle to explain. The quiet response can therefore hide how active the issue still is for you.

Your way back seems to happen in stages. On the night of a disappointing swim, you wanted dinner and no analysis. The next day, looking at one part of the turn with your coach was useful. Quiet time, cooking with music, or walking with one friend can also help. The exact reason each helps is not fully clear, but none requires you to solve everything at once.

It is not yet clear whether this narrowing mainly belongs to sport and visible evaluation or also appears in exams, work, cooking, and friendship problems. Exams are coming up now, and you need more quiet than usual, so this week is carrying extra load. Your present need for space should not be mistaken for your permanent level.
bos_sources.takeaway: When pressure narrows your view, space first and one clear piece later may fit your natural timing.

bos_sources.headline: You lead without taking over
bos_sources.text:
One of your more distinctive strengths is quiet coordination. You listen before acting, but you do not simply wait for someone else forever. When there is no plan, you can offer one. You often phrase direction as something the group can respond to, which lets you create movement without taking all the room.

You connect inclusion with completion. Noticing who has not spoken helps more people enter the work; tracking agreements helps the work continue after the conversation. Asking someone else to check project references shows that you can use another set of eyes while still owning your part. Those actions do more than include people or organize details: they join people awareness with practical follow-through.

The tradeoff is that your leadership may become least visible exactly when it is most needed. Waiting for the perfect opening can let a discussion move on. Softening a proposal too much can make ownership unclear. Because assigning jobs is uncomfortable, you may keep extra coordination in your own hands. You have described this most clearly in groups of peers.

Your competitive side adds firmness to this quieter style. You want to improve and can stick with a considered decision, so making room for others does not mean you lack direction. When the balance works, you protect both the standard and the group. When overused, the same combination can become stubbornness about the decision or too much checking of the standard.
bos_sources.takeaway: You can create direction, inclusion, and follow-through without needing to control the room.

bos_sources.headline: Clear rails, room to breathe
bos_sources.text:
You seem to do best with clear rails rather than a cage. Knowing the week, getting early notice, and seeing a first step help you coordinate school, sport, friendships, and other promises. Because you can rearrange plans, structure is not about keeping everything unchanged. It is about making enough of the shape visible that one part of life does not unexpectedly knock into another.

In learning and feedback, useful detail matters. One example to work through, a reason behind a correction, and a little time to process can help you turn input into your own next step. Public, instant answers may reveal less of your thinking. A direct, private conversation often gives your actual view more room to appear.

You also need a mix of people and unclaimed time. Small groups, close friends, and shared activities can feel connecting; a packed weekend or many last-minute messages can drain you. After dense social or performance time, an evening without plans may restore some room. Cooking with music and walking with one friend are two ways you have said help you feel like yourself again.

Cooking may be especially fitting because it contains both sides of you: recipes, timers, and patient improvement on one side; familiar experimentation and play on the other. Thriving for you is not only quiet, certainty, or routine—you can enjoy team days and try something unfamiliar. The amount of recovery space you need can change with the week, rather than defining you all the time.
bos_sources.takeaway: You need enough structure to coordinate life and enough open space to stay curious, connected, and fully yourself.

bos_sources.headline: Your command pattern
bos_sources.text: You usually listen and make room first, then offer a direction when no plan exists. Your style is collaborative, but a choice you have considered carefully can become firm. You can move a group forward without treating other people’s ideas as obstacles. Waiting for broad agreement may cost you the opening, while a settled decision can become hard to revisit. With peers, you make room before directing; in class, waiting can cost you the chance to speak.
bos_sources.takeaway: You usually listen and make room first, then offer a direction when no plan exists. Your style is collaborative, but a choice you have considered carefully can become firm.

bos_sources.headline: Your tempo pattern
bos_sources.text: You tend to let thoughts form before speaking or committing. Once ready, you can act steadily, but fast exchanges may move beyond your preferred pace. A pause lets you compare options, choose words, and give an answer you can stand behind. Class discussions or instant questions may end before your full view becomes visible. This slower pace shows most in difficult choices, feedback, public questions, and pressure—not in every task.
bos_sources.takeaway: You tend to let thoughts form before speaking or committing. Once ready, you can act steadily, but fast exchanges may move beyond your preferred pace.

bos_sources.headline: Your relational awareness pattern
bos_sources.text: You notice airtime, promises, and how changed plans affect people. You often check by asking or agreeing together rather than assuming you know what everyone wants. You can include quieter voices and protect shared expectations without needing to dominate. Trying not to cause trouble can lead to a quick yes, a late boundary, or extra work for you. Your people focus centers on participation and reliability; it does not mean you catch every subtle signal.
bos_sources.takeaway: You notice airtime, promises, and how changed plans affect people. You often check by asking or agreeing together rather than assuming you know what everyone wants.

bos_sources.headline: Your precision pattern
bos_sources.text: Details and errors pull your attention enough that you check, compare, and refine. Familiarity can loosen this: known recipes become a place to experiment. Examples, timers, review, and repetition can help you protect the parts that truly need accuracy. A small detail can delay sending, starting the next task, or moving on after a mistake. Pressure makes error focus stronger, while familiar cooking is a clear exception to your usual care.
bos_sources.takeaway: Details and errors pull your attention enough that you check, compare, and refine. Familiarity can loosen this: known recipes become a place to experiment.

bos_sources.headline: Your leverage pattern
bos_sources.text: You keep ownership of the work while bringing in focused help: one adviser, example, coach, timer, or second checker. Targeted support gives you a model, another view, or a clearer next independent step. Public asking and assigning work feel less comfortable, so you may still carry more than necessary. This may look different if you are responsible for a large team rather than one piece of shared work.
bos_sources.takeaway: You keep ownership of the work while bringing in focused help: one adviser, example, coach, timer, or second checker.

bos_sources.headline: Your adaptability pattern
bos_sources.text: You like a starting map, but you are not tied to one route. Familiarity, low stakes, and trusted company can make experimenting easier. You can protect the important commitment while changing the route used to meet it. Changes affecting a promise feel costly, and a carefully settled decision may resist reopening. Your flexibility depends strongly on the situation; major new information may test it differently.
bos_sources.takeaway: You like a starting map, but you are not tied to one route. Familiarity, low stakes, and trusted company can make experimenting easier.

bos_sources.headline: Your structure pattern
bos_sources.text: You like visible weeks, written options, and clear agreements. Plans mainly help you coordinate, since you can rearrange them when needed. A visible plan helps commitments coexist and makes hidden clashes easier to catch. Last-minute messages can disrupt several promises at once, especially when detailed checking is already taking time. You show planned flexibility, not a need for every moment to stay unchanged.
bos_sources.takeaway: You like visible weeks, written options, and clear agreements. Plans mainly help you coordinate, since you can rearrange them when needed.

bos_sources.headline: Your perspective pattern
bos_sources.text: You connect present choices with later effects on sport, people, money, work, and time. More than one future can stay active after you choose. You can look beyond the nearest reward and protect several important parts of life. The cost of the unchosen option can turn useful reflection into second-guessing. Your longer-range ideas about sport and cooking are still open, so this outlook is exploratory rather than settled.
bos_sources.takeaway: You connect present choices with later effects on sport, people, money, work, and time. More than one future can stay active after you choose.

The coach said they would show one turn focus, choose the technical cue after reviewing the example, observe the next length, and use five minutes of the existing Monday review without adding pool time (COACH2, COACH3). The coach also plans the pool sessions (A06), supporting the proposed request to choose a planned set.

The shorter action headline accurately states the initiating action—asking the coach for one clear turn focus—while the adjacent when and who fields supply the demonstration, set selection, observation, and check-in details. It does not claim that the request has already been accepted or completed.

The timing and sequencing are clear. September 21, 2026 is the confirmed Monday review and is used for setup. A same-session test is conditional on agreement; otherwise, the athlete only proposes using the existing Tuesday, September 22 session. The usefulness check occurs only after the agreed set. No clock time or guaranteed opportunity is introduced.

Progress remains untested when required. The review expressly states that no set or no check-in leaves the result untested, so setup completion is not confused with evidence of progress or usefulness.

Observation and internal experience are correctly separated. The coach reports what was externally observed about continuing into the next length, while the athlete reports whether the focus was recognized and whether attention became caught in additional checking. The coach is not assigned knowledge of the athlete’s internal thoughts or feelings.

Coach participation is explicitly requested rather than presumed: “Could you…” frames the demonstration, set choice, and observation as a proposal; the set and check-in must be agreed; and without agreement the test waits. The coach’s technical authority is consistent with COACH2 and COACH3.

The possible reset remains conditional and unagreed. The athlete is told to ask about testing one brief reminder only if the turn focus is clear but replay continues. This does not claim that a reset has been selected, accepted, tested, or effective, consistent with A14 and COACH3.
The revisions introduce no clock time, guaranteed training opportunity, performance promise, outcome claim, or medical claim.

The revised opening is source-faithful. Quiet competitiveness and the personal-best aim are supported by A02 and A11; the lack of interest in being the center of attention is supported by BOS:identity and BOS:effort. Beginning from a concrete example and then applying or adapting it is supported across swimming by A08, maths by A17–A18 and BOS:mind, and cooking by BOS:mind, BOS:effort and BOS:adaptability.

The short action headline accurately identifies the central first move—asking the coach for one turn focus. The adjacent when and who fields supply the necessary follow-through of selecting an existing set, naming an observable sign and arranging a check-in, so the shorter headline does not conceal a materially different action.

The new coach roles are supported and appropriately bounded. A06 establishes that the coach plans the pool sessions; COACH2 supports the coach selecting the technical cue, showing the focus and observing the next length; and COACH3 supports using five minutes of the existing Monday review and providing one written cue. Naming a visible sign is framed as something the athlete asks the coach to do, not as an already completed agreement.

The proposed arrangement is not represented as an existing agreement or outcome. The athlete is told to ask the coach, same-session testing is conditional on agreement, setup remains pending without the agreements, and the test waits without agreement. This is consistent with A15 and with COACH3's statement that no reset has yet been chosen or agreed.

The timing and review sequence are coherent. September 21 is the confirmed Monday review date and is used first for setup; a trial can occur later in that existing Monday session only if agreed. September 22 is correctly treated as the existing Tuesday-session alternative and only as a proposal. No clock time or guaranteed testing opportunity is invented.

Setup and usefulness are clearly separated. September 21 first checks whether the focus, existing set, visible sign and after-set check-in have been agreed. Usefulness is checked only after an agreed set, either on September 21 or conditionally on September 22.

Observation and internal experience remain separate. The coach reports the observable next-length behavior, consistent with COACH2, while the athlete reports recognizing the focus or becoming caught in extra checking, consistent with A04 and A09. The patch does not claim that the coach knows what the athlete thinks or feels.

The untested state is explicit: if the set or check-in does not occur, usefulness remains untested. The edits add no unsupported split, clock time, guaranteed opportunity, result, performance promise or medical claim.
